stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old boy after five days of unremitting fever to 39.6 degrees Celsius. His mother reports he has been miserable, not eating, and his eyes have become red without any discharge. On examination you find a diffuse maculopapular rash across the trunk, an erythematous strawberry tongue with cracked lips, and a single tender left cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm. His hands and feet are firm and swollen with a dusky red hue over the palms and soles. There is no pus behind the tonsils. His BCG scar is inflamed. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 18.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 542 x10^9/L (150-400), CRP 148 mg/L (<5), ESR 78 mm/h (<15), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), ALT 78 U/L (<40)
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection with limbic sparing, brawny oedema of dorsum of hands and feet, injected pharynx without exudate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus anti-inflammatory-dose aspirin now
options.rationale: The child meets classic Kawasaki disease criteria: fever five days or more plus at least four of five principal features (bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oropharyngeal changes with strawberry tongue and cracked lips, extremity changes with firm swelling, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5 cm). Sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytosis after day 7 and the inflamed BCG scar support the diagnosis. Australian and RCH guidance is IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion within 10 days of fever onset to reduce coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%, plus aspirin at anti-inflammatory doses (30-50 mg/kg/day) until afebrile for 48-72 hours then low-dose antiplatelet. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin plus paired blood cultures for suspected scalded skin syndrome
options.rationale: SSSS causes generalised superficial desquamation with a positive Nikolsky sign and painful skin, not conjunctivitis with strawberry tongue and extremity oedema. Blood cultures would not be first-line here and flucloxacillin does not address the vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin 33 mg/kg every 8 hours for scarlet fever and general practice review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Scarlet fever from group A streptococcus can share the strawberry tongue and rash but presents with painful pharyngitis, exudative tonsils, and a sandpaper rash rather than five days of fever with bilateral conjunctivitis and extremity oedema. Kawasaki disease requires urgent IVIG within the 10-day treatment window. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone plus oral amoxicillin for likely bacterial cervical adenitis
options.rationale: Isolated cervical adenitis does not explain the multi-system findings and rash. Antibiotic monotherapy for a suspected bacterial neck infection would miss the diagnosis and delay coronary-protective IVIG. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Reassure the family this is a viral exanthem and discharge with oral fluid and paracetamol advice
options.rationale: Five days of fever with bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes, extremity oedema, polymorphous rash and cervical adenopathy fulfil Kawasaki criteria and mandate hospital treatment. Missing the window increases coronary aneurysm risk substantially. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

explanation.summary: This child fulfils fever plus four of five classic Kawasaki criteria on day five, with laboratory features (thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria, transaminitis) that raise the pre-test probability further. IVIG 2 g/kg within 10 days of fever onset is the coronary-protective intervention. High-dose aspirin is added for anti-inflammatory effect. A baseline echocardiogram is performed on admission.
key_points: Fever 5+ days plus 4/5 principal criteria diagnoses Kawasaki (incomplete Kawasaki uses labs)
IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion within 10 days reduces aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~4%
High-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day until afebrile then 3-5 mg/kg antiplatelet dose
Baseline echocardiogram on diagnosis; repeat at 2 and 6 weeks
explanation.pearls: IVIG dose 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours as one infusion; if fever persists 36 hours after infusion, repeat IVIG plus consider methylprednisolone or infliximab.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-month-old infant with a 2-day history of coryza and worsening cough. He was born at term and is otherwise well. Feeding has dropped to 40% of usual over the last 12 hours. Wet nappies remain regular. On admission at 22:00 you commenced nasal prong oxygen at 1 litre per minute for SpO2 of 87% and moderate work of breathing. It is now 00:15. The nurse reports his SpO2 has settled at 90%, respiratory rate has come down from 68 to 56, and he took 60 mL of formula 45 minutes ago without vomiting. Chest examination reveals widespread wheeze and fine crackles bilaterally with mild subcostal recession.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, respiratory rate 56, SpO2 90% on nasal prong 1 L/min, temperature 37.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Work of breathing: Mild subcostal recession, no head bob, no grunt, alert and consolable
data_table.Feeding: 60 mL of 90 mL feed taken 45 minutes ago, no vomiting, 3 wet nappies in last 12 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate to high-flow nasal cannula humidified oxygen at 2 L/kg/min inspired flow now
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance reserves HFNC for infants who fail to improve on low-flow oxygen after 1 to 2 hours, defined as persistent hypoxia despite low-flow, worsening work of breathing, or increasing respiratory rate. This infant is stable on low-flow with SpO2 within the acceptable target range and improving respiratory rate, so premature escalation adds no benefit while consuming a scarce resource. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Continue nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and reassess response 1 hour after commencing oxygen
options.rationale: RCH bronchiolitis guidance targets SpO2 90% or above, uses nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen, and formally reassesses at 1 to 2 hours. This infant has met target saturation, respiratory rate is trending down, work of breathing is mild, and enteral feeding is tolerated. Continuing the current plan and reassessing is the correct action. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment of work of breathing 20 minutes later
options.rationale: Bronchodilators are not recommended for bronchiolitis under 12 months. AAP and RCH advise against routine salbutamol, which does not improve length of stay, oxygen requirement, or admission rate in bronchiolitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Switch to nasogastric feeds at 100 mL/kg/day and cease all oral feeding for 24 hours
options.rationale: NGT feeding is indicated for bronchiolitis when work of breathing is moderate to severe, respiratory rate exceeds 60 sustained on oxygen, oral intake drops below 50% of maintenance, or the infant cannot coordinate suck and breath. This infant just took a full feed volume and has improving work of breathing. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Wean nasal prong oxygen off completely and check room-air saturations 10 minutes later
options.rationale: The infant is only 2.5 hours into oxygen therapy and remains on 1 L/min to hold SpO2 at 90%. Trials off oxygen are typically considered after sustained SpO2 above 92% on minimal supplemental oxygen with settled work of breathing, usually the following morning. Weaning now is premature. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH bronchiolitis pathway uses low-flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min as first-line oxygen with SpO2 target of 90% or above. Escalation to HFNC is reserved for treatment failure at 1 to 2 hours defined by hypoxia despite low-flow, increasing work of breathing or rising respiratory rate. Bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not routinely indicated. Feeding assessment guides transition to nasogastric feeds.
key_points: SpO2 target 90% (not 92-94%) for bronchiolitis under 12 months per RCH
Low-flow nasal prong 1-2 L/min is first-line oxygen; HFNC only for low-flow failure at 1-2 hours
Bronchodilators, corticosteroids and adrenaline nebulisers not routinely recommended
NGT feeds if intake <50% of maintenance or moderate/severe work of breathing
explanation.pearls: Do not use HFNC as a first-line escalation. RCH audit found 32% of HFNC starts were premature; low-flow held saturations in 68%.

stem: You are the paediatric intern reviewing a 3-hour-old term male on the postnatal ward. His mother has diet-controlled gestational diabetes and he weighed 4310 g at birth (95th centile). He has fed well twice on the breast since delivery. The midwife checked a pre-feed blood sugar because of his birthweight. He is pink, alert and rooting for a feed. Temperature is stable, tone is normal, and there is no jitteriness or respiratory distress. There are no other risk factors. The bedside meter reads 1.9 mmol/L; a paired laboratory sample has been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Feeding: Two effective breastfeeds since birth, latching well, no vomits, no jitters
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L (>=2.6), paired plasma glucose pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother the reading is expected in the first 24 hours and simply repeat the pre-feed check
options.rationale: Neonatal blood glucose below 2.6 mmol/L in an at-risk infant requires action, not observation. The infant of a diabetic mother and a large-for-gestational-age infant are both listed at-risk groups by RCH and the ADIPS/NICE-derived Australian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give an intravenous bolus of 10% dextrose 2.5 mL/kg and admit the infant to the special care nursery
options.rationale: IV dextrose bolus 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia (jitteriness, seizures, apnoea, poor tone) or blood glucose persistently below 1.5 mmol/L despite feeds and buccal dextrose gel. This asymptomatic infant with a modestly low reading warrants a staged feed-and-gel approach first. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate breastfeed and recheck 30 minutes after feeding
options.rationale: For asymptomatic infants in an at-risk category with blood glucose 1.5 to 2.5 mmol/L, RCH and the Sugar Babies trial pathway recommend 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) massaged into the buccal mucosa with an immediate feed, followed by a repeat blood glucose 30 minutes after the feed. This halves the rate of admission for IV dextrose. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Commence donor expressed breast milk 20 mL/kg/day by nasogastric tube and skip the maternal breastfeed
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding removes the strongest driver of postnatal glucose stabilisation. Buccal gel plus continued direct breastfeeding is preferred; NGT feeds are reserved for infants unable to feed effectively at the breast or bottle. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Wait for the paired laboratory plasma glucose result before acting because bedside meters are inaccurate
options.rationale: Point-of-care meters are known to be less accurate at extreme lows, but pathway guidance is to act on the bedside reading in a well infant while a paired sample is being processed, because delayed treatment risks neurological injury if the true glucose is low. Confirmatory sampling is drawn at the same time, not awaited before intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: The at-risk term infant with asymptomatic hypoglycaemia between 1.5 and 2.5 mmol/L should receive 40% dextrose buccal gel 200 mg/kg with an immediate feed. The Sugar Babies protocol reduces NICU admissions and preserves breastfeeding. Symptomatic infants or those with blood glucose below 1.5 mmol/L go straight to IV dextrose bolus.
key_points: Blood glucose <2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, preterm) triggers action
Asymptomatic 1.5-2.5 mmol/L: 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) buccal plus feed
Symptomatic OR <1.5 mmol/L: 10% dextrose IV bolus 2 mL/kg then infusion 60 mL/kg/day
Recheck glucose 30 minutes after feed following gel
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dose is 200 mg/kg = 0.5 mL/kg; maximum two doses in 24 hours before escalating to IV.

stem: You are the obstetric registrar assessing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 39+4 weeks who presents in early labour. She had a normal vaginal delivery at term two years ago. Her antenatal course has been unremarkable. A vaginal-rectal swab at 36+2 weeks was positive for Group B streptococcus. She has no drug allergies. Cervical examination reveals 4 cm dilated, 90% effaced, membranes intact. Contractions are every 4 minutes lasting 45 seconds. Foetal heart rate baseline is 140 with normal variability and accelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal HR 140
data_table.Cervical exam: 4 cm dilated, 90% effaced, station -1, membranes intact
data_table.History: GBS positive vaginal-rectal swab at 36+2 weeks, no penicillin allergy, no previous GBS-affected infant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 500 mg every 8 hours until delivery for group B streptococcus prophylaxis
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve intrapartum tissue and cord blood concentrations sufficient to reduce early-onset GBS neonatal disease. Australian and CDC-based intrapartum protocols require IV therapy. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g at the start of the active labour phase
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not the recommended IAP agent and single dosing does not maintain adequate cord blood concentrations across the intrapartum period. Serial IV doses of benzylpenicillin are used. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until delivery for group B streptococcus prophylaxis
options.rationale: Clindamycin is reserved for women with severe penicillin allergy where the isolate has documented clindamycin susceptibility. In an unallergic woman, benzylpenicillin is first-line because of superior efficacy and narrower spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic GBS IAP)

options.text: Give intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery
options.rationale: Australian RANZCOG guidance and Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommend IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery for GBS-positive women without penicillin allergy, aiming for at least 4 hours of exposure before delivery to reduce early-onset GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and reassess if the maternal temperature rises above 37.8 degrees Celsius
options.rationale: GBS-positive status alone (not intrapartum fever) is the indication for IAP. Waiting for fever misses the window to reduce vertical transmission and early-onset neonatal disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Universal antenatal screening at 35 to 37 weeks or a risk-based approach identifies women needing intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. In a penicillin-tolerant woman with a positive antenatal swab, IV benzylpenicillin loading 3 g followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours is the RANZCOG-endorsed regimen. Adequate prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours between the first dose and delivery.
key_points: GBS positive swab at 35-37 weeks = IAP in labour or ROM at term
Benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth
Cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours if non-severe penicillin allergy
Clindamycin only if severe pen allergy AND documented isolate susceptibility
explanation.pearls: Adequate IAP defined as at least one dose of benzylpenicillin 4 hours or more before delivery; shorter intervals still confer some but reduced benefit.

stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G1P0 in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhoea and 3 days of intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort but no heavy bleeding. She has no significant medical history, no allergies, and lives locally with her partner. She works as a primary school teacher and is highly reliable for follow-up. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 26 mm right adnexal mass containing no embryonic pole, no cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG today is 4820 IU/L; a value 48 hours ago at another service was 4180 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed with minimal spotting
data_table.Investigations: bhCG 4820 IU/L today (was 4180 IU/L 48 h ago), Hb 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 258 x10^9/L, LFTs normal, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), transvaginal US 26 mm right adnexal mass without cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin every 48 hours in the outpatient setting
options.rationale: Expectant management is confined to a small subset with bhCG less than 1000 IU/L, a decreasing trend, no adnexal mass or cardiac activity, and no pain. This woman has a rising bhCG above 4800 IU/L with an adnexal mass and pain, so expectant management fails RANZCOG criteria. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
options.rationale: The RANZCOG threshold requiring surgical management is bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher, or the presence of cardiac activity, mass 3.5 cm or larger, significant pain, haemodynamic instability, or unreliable follow-up. This woman meets none of the mandatory surgical triggers. Salpingectomy is also more invasive than methotrexate when the tube-sparing medical option remains available. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopic salpingostomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
options.rationale: Salpingostomy has higher rates of persistent trophoblast and is largely reserved for cases where the contralateral tube is absent or diseased. Neither medical nor surgical thresholds mandate this approach for the current presentation. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Administer oral mifepristone 200 mg now followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 microgram 48 hours later
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is a medical termination regimen for intrauterine pregnancy and does not treat tubal ectopic. Trophoblast in the tube will continue to grow and risk rupture. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

options.text: Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 beta-hCG monitoring
options.rationale: This woman meets Australian RANZCOG criteria for medical management with single-dose methotrexate: bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, no significant pain, haemodynamically stable, reliable for follow-up, no contraindications with normal baseline haematology, renal and liver function. Single-dose 50 mg per m2 IM is standard with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (expect >=15% fall from day 4 to day 7) and weekly bhCG thereafter. (Source: RANZCOG GPS: Tubal ectopic pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable woman with a tubal ectopic pregnancy meeting RANZCOG criteria: bhCG less than 5000 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, mass smaller than 3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, and no contraindications. Success rates approximate 85 to 90% with these thresholds. Failure of bhCG to fall by 15% between day 4 and day 7 triggers a second dose or surgical intervention.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: bhCG <5000, no cardiac activity, mass <3.5 cm, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, no CI
Single-dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with day 4 and day 7 bhCG (>=15% fall required)
Surgical management mandated at bhCG >=5000 IU/L or cardiac activity or mass >=3.5 cm or instability
Contraindications include cytopenias, abnormal LFTs, creatinine >120, breastfeeding, hepatic or renal disease
explanation.pearls: The RANZCOG surgical threshold for tubal ectopic is bhCG >=5000 IU/L (not 3000). Methotrexate remains an option below 5000 with all other criteria met.

stem: A 57-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with a 12-month history of vaginal dryness, dyspareunia and post-coital spotting. Her last menstrual period was 5 years ago. She had breast cancer at age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive) treated with mastectomy, chemotherapy and trastuzumab, with no evidence of recurrence and current oncology sign-off for symptom management. She is otherwise well. She has already trialled a non-hormonal water-based lubricant and a polycarbophil vaginal moisturiser three times weekly for 3 months with only partial relief. She has no urinary symptoms and speculum examination shows pale, thin vaginal walls with loss of rugae, no discharge, and healthy cervix. There is no bleeding after speculum removal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 130/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Vaginal walls pale, thin, loss of rugae, minor petechial contact bleeding, no ulceration or lesion; cervix visible, no discharge
data_table.History: Breast cancer age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive), post-chemo, oncology sign-off given for local symptom therapy, no VTE history, no current medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe estriol 0.03 mg vaginal pessary daily for 2 weeks then twice-weekly maintenance dosing
options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal estrogens (estradiol 10 microgram tablets or estriol 0.03 mg pessaries) produce local mucosal restoration with minimal systemic absorption and are supported by the AMS and RANZCOG for genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Recent evidence and IMS 2016 statement support use in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement after non-hormonal therapies fail. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Commence combined oral hormone therapy estradiol 1 mg plus micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
options.rationale: Systemic hormone therapy is inappropriate for isolated genitourinary symptoms and carries risks even in ER-negative disease that are hard to justify when a low-dose local option addresses the symptom directly. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Commence oral ospemifene 60 mg daily and arrange in-person symptom review at 6 to 8 weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Ospemifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator not routinely available on the PBS in Australia and generally avoided in women with prior breast cancer because of uncertain breast safety. AMS advises against SERM use in breast cancer survivors. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Refer for fractional carbon dioxide vaginal laser therapy as first-line after moisturiser failure
options.rationale: Vaginal laser therapy is not first-line and lacks the evidence base for efficacy and safety endorsed by the AMS and TGA; the TGA issued a safety alert in 2018. Reserve for after trial of local estrogen with oncology input. (Source: AMS: Vulvovaginal atrophy)

options.text: Refer for outpatient cervical biopsy plus office hysteroscopy to exclude endometrial pathology today
options.rationale: Post-coital spotting from a friable atrophic vagina with a normal cervix does not itself mandate hysteroscopy; if postmenopausal bleeding is truly unexplained after treatment of atrophy or if endometrium is thickened on ultrasound (>4 mm), then endometrial assessment is warranted. Directly biopsying without addressing the atrophic cause first is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCOG PMB)

explanation.summary: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause with failure of non-hormonal therapy is treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen. Australian AMS guidance supports this option in ER-negative breast cancer survivors with oncology agreement. Systemic HRT is disproportionate for local symptoms and ospemifene is not first-line in Australia.
key_points: Non-hormonal moisturiser and lubricant trial is first-line for GSM
Vaginal estradiol 10 mcg tablet or estriol 0.03 mg pessary, daily loading then twice-weekly maintenance
Local estrogen is acceptable in most breast cancer survivors after oncology discussion
Vaginal laser therapy is not endorsed as first-line by AMS or TGA
explanation.pearls: Systemic absorption from low-dose vaginal estradiol tablets rarely exceeds baseline postmenopausal serum estradiol; onc consent still documented case-by-case.

stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman in outpatient clinic. She was diagnosed with a first episode of moderate major depressive disorder 14 weeks ago. She commenced sertraline titrated over 6 weeks to 150 mg daily, which she has taken consistently for 8 weeks at the current dose with clear improvement in initiation and appetite but persistent hopelessness, anhedonia and suicidal ideation without plan. PHQ-9 has moved from 20 to 14. Sleep initiation is poor. She tolerates sertraline without side effects, has no active substance use, and completes weekly individual CBT with fidelity. There is no bipolar family history and no manic features. Baseline blood pressure is 118/76.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 42 mcg/L (30-300), vitamin B12 380 pmol/L (>200)
data_table.History: Sertraline 150 mg daily for 8 weeks at target dose, weekly CBT with a psychologist, PHQ-9 20 -> 14 with persistent hopelessness and suicidal ideation, no bipolarity, no substances, no thyroid or cardiac disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 200 mg daily and review response at four weeks in clinic
options.rationale: Sertraline shows a flat dose-response above 150 to 200 mg for antidepressant effect, and dose escalation beyond an already therapeutic dose that has been trialled for 8 weeks confers little additional benefit relative to switch or augmentation strategies. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Cross-taper sertraline to venlafaxine extended-release and titrate to 225 mg daily over three weeks
options.rationale: After an adequate SSRI trial (at least 4 weeks at target dose) with partial response, RANZCP and STAR-D data support switching to a serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor such as venlafaxine. Cross-tapering avoids withdrawal, and titration to 225 mg daily engages noradrenergic mechanism absent with SSRI. Blood pressure monitoring is required as venlafaxine can raise BP dose-dependently. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

options.text: Add fluoxetine 20 mg daily to the current sertraline regimen as combination antidepressant therapy
options.rationale: Combining two SSRIs offers no additional benefit and substantially increases the risk of serotonin syndrome, particularly with fluoxetine's long half-life. This is contraindicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Add tranylcypromine 10 mg daily on top of the current sertraline for augmentation of antidepressant effect
options.rationale: Combining an SSRI with a non-selective irreversible MAOI is contraindicated because of catastrophic serotonin syndrome risk. A washout of 5 to 6 weeks after fluoxetine or 2 weeks after most other SSRIs is required before starting an MAOI. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: MAOIs)

options.text: Cease sertraline abruptly and start amitriptyline 25 mg nightly the next day for treatment-resistant depression
options.rationale: Abrupt SSRI cessation risks discontinuation syndrome, and starting a TCA without cross-taper and without addressing suicidality with a monitoring plan is unsafe. Amitriptyline is also more lethal in overdose than SSRIs or SNRIs. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: After a partial response to an adequate SSRI trial, RANZCP guidance and STAR-D data support either switching to another class such as an SNRI, or augmenting with lithium, second-generation antipsychotic, or a psychological therapy. Venlafaxine XR to 225 mg engages noradrenergic mechanism absent from SSRIs. Blood pressure and adherence are monitored during titration.
key_points: Adequate SSRI trial = target dose for at least 4 weeks; here 8 weeks at 150 mg satisfies
Partial response at adequate SSRI trial -> switch class (SNRI, mirtazapine) or augment (lithium, quetiapine, aripiprazole)
Venlafaxine XR requires BP monitoring; target 225 mg for treatment-resistant depression
SSRI + MAOI and SSRI + SSRI combinations are contraindicated (serotonin syndrome)
explanation.pearls: Cross-taper duration for sertraline to venlafaxine is typically 2 weeks: reduce sertraline by 50 mg per week while introducing venlafaxine 37.5 mg then increasing weekly.

stem: You are the medical registrar admitting a 48-year-old man for elective alcohol detoxification. He has been drinking 20 standard drinks per day for 8 years. His last drink was 14 hours ago. He has a history of tonic-clonic seizure during a prior unassisted withdrawal 3 years ago but no delirium tremens. He is medically stable, taking no other substances, and has no benzodiazepine tolerance issues. On admission examination he is tremulous with mild diaphoresis, orientated to person, place and time, and following commands. His CIWA-Ar score is currently 12 and rising over the last 2 hours. He weighs 82 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate 0.7 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), LFTs mildly deranged with AST 92 U/L (<35), platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), thiamine and B12 not yet measured
data_table.History: Prior tonic-clonic seizure during unassisted withdrawal, no prior DTs, no other substances, no allergies, weight 82 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Give oral haloperidol 5 mg now and repeat every 4 hours as required for withdrawal-associated agitation
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are not first-line for alcohol withdrawal. They are added only when psychotic features persist despite adequate benzodiazepine loading, not as monotherapy. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Commence phenytoin 15 mg/kg intravenous loading dose to prevent further alcohol-withdrawal seizures
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures. Adequate benzodiazepine dosing is the seizure-preventive agent of choice in alcohol withdrawal. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Give parenteral thiamine 300 mg then symptom-triggered diazepam by CIWA-Ar with a scheduled loading dose
options.rationale: Australian withdrawal guidance is symptom-triggered benzodiazepine (diazepam) titrated to CIWA-Ar with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Prior withdrawal seizure raises baseline risk, so a scheduled front-loading dose of diazepam 20 mg is added on top of the CIWA-Ar protocol. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Prescribe fixed-dose oral diazepam 5 mg every 6 hours regardless of the current CIWA-Ar score
options.rationale: Fixed low-dose scheduling under-treats moderate withdrawal and is associated with higher seizure rates than symptom-triggered dosing. Symptom-triggered dosing tailored to the CIWA-Ar score is the current standard. (Source: NSW Health Alcohol Withdrawal Guideline)

options.text: Commence oral naltrexone 50 mg daily now and continue CIWA-Ar assessment every 4 hours through withdrawal
options.rationale: Naltrexone is a relapse-prevention agent commenced after withdrawal is complete, not during acute withdrawal. It has no role in symptom control during the acute withdrawal period. (Source: RACGP Alcohol Use Disorder)

explanation.summary: Australian alcohol withdrawal guidance uses symptom-triggered diazepam titrated to a validated withdrawal scale (CIWA-Ar) as the cornerstone. Parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV or IM is given before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy in this population. A prior withdrawal seizure is a clear indication for a scheduled loading dose of diazepam in addition to CIWA-driven dosing. Electrolyte replacement (magnesium, phosphate, potassium) is performed early.
key_points: Symptom-triggered diazepam via CIWA-Ar is first-line for moderate to severe withdrawal
Thiamine 300 mg IV/IM before any glucose infusion in AUD to prevent Wernicke
Prior withdrawal seizure warrants scheduled loading dose (e.g. diazepam 20 mg) in addition to symptom-triggered protocol
Replace magnesium, phosphate, potassium; monitor for arrhythmia risk
explanation.pearls: Wernicke prophylaxis is 300 mg IV/IM thiamine daily for 3 days; a Wernicke-suspected patient requires 500 mg IV three times daily for 2-3 days.

stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 46-year-old woman who wants to stop smoking. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day, smokes her first cigarette within 15 minutes of waking, and has a Fagerstrom score of 8. Two previous quit attempts using nicotine patches alone lasted 3 and 5 weeks before relapse. She has a history of depression, currently in stable remission on sertraline 100 mg for 3 years without recent low mood or suicidal thoughts. She has no history of psychosis, seizure or eating disorder. She has read about all three PBS-listed cessation agents and asks for the most effective option for her.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, LFTs normal, renal function normal, PHQ-9 4 (minimal), sertraline 100 mg stable for 3 years
data_table.History: 30 cigarettes per day, first cigarette within 15 minutes, Fagerstrom 8, two prior patch monotherapy relapses at 3 and 5 weeks, depression in remission, no psychosis, no seizure, no eating disorder, no pregnancy risk

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is most appropriate as monotherapy for this attempt?

options.text: Continue nicotine 21 mg patch monotherapy as previously and review symptoms weekly in general practice
options.rationale: Patch monotherapy has already failed twice and Fagerstrom 8 indicates high nicotine dependence. Repeating the same intervention that has previously failed offers a lower success rate than switching to a more effective agent or adding short-acting NRT to combination therapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg once daily for six days then 150 mg twice daily as monotherapy for 12 weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in current SSRI use because of serotonin syndrome and seizure risk concerns; while she is only on sertraline, the RACGP prefers not to combine bupropion with an SSRI when other equally effective options exist. Varenicline also has higher cessation rates than bupropion (approximately 33% vs 24% at 12 months). (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Nortriptyline 25 mg nightly titrated to 75 to 100 mg nightly with ECG check before dose escalation
options.rationale: Nortriptyline has cessation efficacy but is second-line in Australia and adds cardiac and anticholinergic risks; RACGP reserves it for when first-line agents cannot be used. Interaction risk with sertraline (QT and serotonergic) also disfavours it here. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Varenicline titrated to 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, starting 1 to 2 weeks before target quit date
options.rationale: Varenicline has the highest 12-month abstinence rate of the three PBS-listed monotherapies. RACGP now advises varenicline is safe in stable depression, with pooled trial data showing no increased neuropsychiatric adverse events versus placebo. It is a partial nicotinic agonist that both reduces cravings and blocks smoking reward. Titration reduces nausea. She should set a quit date 1 to 2 weeks after starting therapy. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

options.text: Nicotine mouth spray as sole short-acting nicotine replacement therapy for 12 weeks after quit date
options.rationale: Short-acting NRT monotherapy is less effective than varenicline or NRT combination therapy for someone with high Fagerstrom dependence. Short-acting NRT is typically paired with patch as combination NRT for heavy smokers. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation guideline)

explanation.summary: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation in Australian PBS-listed options, achieving approximately 33% 12-month continuous abstinence versus 24% for bupropion and 20% for single-agent NRT. Historical FDA warnings about neuropsychiatric events were removed in 2016 after the EAGLES trial found no increased risk. It is appropriate for a person with high-dependence smoking and stable depression on an SSRI.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation (12-month abstinence ~33%)
Combination NRT (patch + short-acting) is equally effective and useful when varenicline is contraindicated
Varenicline titrated over 7 days to 1 mg twice daily; quit date 1-2 weeks after starting
Stable psychiatric illness is not a contraindication (EAGLES 2016)
explanation.pearls: Varenicline plus NRT combination has some evidence for higher abstinence than either alone but is not yet PBS-endorsed combination therapy; use varenicline alone at 1 mg BD.

stem: You are the medical registrar in an Australian metropolitan emergency department reviewing a 62-year-old man with 4 days of productive cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, fever and progressive breathlessness. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His medications are metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin. He is not immunocompromised. He lives independently and has had no recent hospital admissions or overseas travel. He is up to date with pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. On examination he has bronchial breathing in the right mid-zone and dullness to percussion. Chest radiograph shows dense right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 91% on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: white cells 15.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 168 mg/L (<5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), urea 9.1 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2), albumin 34 g/L (35-50), venous pH 7.36 (7.35-7.45), chest radiograph right middle-lobe consolidation without effusion
data_table.History: T2DM, hypertension, up to date pneumococcal and influenza, lives independently, no recent hospitalisation, no travel, no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen and disposition?

options.text: Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 1 g every 8 hours for 5 days with general practitioner review at 48 hours
options.rationale: SMART-COP score is at least 3 (S=0 systolic 108, M=1 multilobar, A=1 albumin 34, R=1 respiratory rate 28, T=0, C=0, O=1 SpO2 91%, P=1 pH not <7.35 so 0) placing him in moderate to high risk. Discharging home understates severity. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy at 1 g daily is used for uncomplicated moderate CAP requiring admission in some Australian guidelines, but the correct benzylpenicillin plus doxycycline combination is the Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic recommendation for moderate CAP without severe features. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or when benzylpenicillin is contraindicated. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to intensive care on intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus intravenous vancomycin loading dose
options.rationale: Broad-spectrum coverage is reserved for severe CAP requiring ICU support (SMART-COP >=5) or high-risk features such as recent hospitalisation, aspiration risk with structural lung disease, or bronchiectasis. This patient does not meet these criteria. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on oral clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 hours as macrolide monotherapy for 5 days total
options.rationale: Macrolide monotherapy is inadequate for moderate CAP in Australia because of high pneumococcal resistance. Australian guidance uses beta-lactam plus atypical cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

options.text: Admit to ward on intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic first-line therapy for moderate CAP requiring admission is IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg BD (or oral clarithromycin) to cover atypicals. SMART-COP score of at least 3 places him in the moderate-to-high risk group warranting admission and IV therapy with switch to oral after 48 hours if improving. (Source: eTG Antibiotic CAP)

explanation.summary: Moderate community-acquired pneumonia in Australia (SMART-COP 3 to 4) requires hospital admission and combination antibiotic therapy targeting pneumococcus and atypical organisms. IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline is the Therapeutic Guidelines first-line regimen. Ceftriaxone is reserved for severe CAP or beta-lactam alternatives; broader-spectrum agents for ICU-level severity or specific risk factors.
key_points: SMART-COP >=3 = moderate; >=5 = severe warranting ICU consideration
Moderate CAP: IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g q6h + doxycycline 100 mg BD
Severe CAP or ICU: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (moxifloxacin if pen allergy)
Switch to oral after 48 hours of clinical improvement; total 5-7 days
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP awards 2 points each for systolic <90 mmHg, SpO2 <=90%, and pH <7.35 (all considered severe features), 1 point each for the other criteria. Score >=3 predicts intensive respiratory or vasopressor support.

stem: You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man 3 months after diagnosis of a right proximal femoral vein deep vein thrombosis. The DVT occurred 4 weeks after right total knee replacement with a 6-week postoperative period of significantly reduced mobility. He has no family history of thrombosis, no prior VTE, no active malignancy, no antiphospholipid syndrome, and no ongoing prothrombotic risk factors. He has completed 3 months of apixaban 5 mg twice daily without bleeding, has walked without ongoing swelling for the past 6 weeks, and has returned to normal daily activity. He asks how long he needs to remain on anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 72, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (135-170), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m2, LFTs within normal limits, D-dimer not indicated at this time
data_table.History: 3 months of apixaban 5 mg BD after post-arthroplasty proximal DVT, no ongoing bleeding, no residual swelling for 6 weeks, no personal or family thrombotic history, no cancer or APS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from today?

options.text: Stop apixaban now and provide written advice on venous thromboembolism prevention for future surgery
options.rationale: This is a proximal DVT clearly provoked by a major transient risk factor (total knee replacement with post-operative immobility). Australian and international haematology guidance (Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand; ASH 2020) recommend cessation of anticoagulation at 3 months in this scenario because the annual recurrence risk after stopping is under 3%, similar to the annual major bleeding risk on ongoing therapy. Patient counselling about recognition of recurrence and future perioperative prophylaxis is essential. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely as extended anticoagulation for the proximal deep vein thrombosis
options.rationale: Indefinite anticoagulation is reserved for unprovoked DVT, active cancer-associated VTE, or recurrent VTE. A proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor does not meet indefinite therapy criteria and exposes the patient to unnecessary bleeding risk. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily and continue indefinitely as extended prophylactic anticoagulation
options.rationale: The extended low-dose apixaban regimen (2.5 mg BD after initial 6 months) is used for unprovoked VTE where the decision is to continue anticoagulation but reduce bleeding risk. It does not apply to a clearly provoked VTE where cessation is preferred at 3 months. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended venous thromboembolism recurrence prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin has been studied for extended VTE prevention (ASPIRE, WARFASA) with only modest recurrence reduction and is inferior to DOAC continuation. It is not the standard approach after cessation of anticoagulation for a provoked DVT and adds bleeding risk without clear benefit here. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily for a further 3 months then stop and provide written VTE advice
options.rationale: Extending anticoagulation to 6 months for a proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor confers no reduction in long-term recurrence relative to 3 months and adds bleeding exposure. Total therapy of 3 months is the standard duration. (Source: THANZ VTE guidelines)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation duration for VTE depends on whether the event was provoked by a major transient factor (surgery, hospitalisation, trauma), a persistent factor, cancer, or unprovoked. Proximal DVT provoked by a major transient factor is treated for 3 months and stopped. Unprovoked or persistent-risk-factor VTE is considered for indefinite therapy weighing bleeding risk. Cancer-associated VTE typically receives extended DOAC or LMWH while the cancer is active.
key_points: Proximal DVT with major transient provoking factor -> 3 months anticoagulation then stop
Unprovoked proximal DVT -> at least 3 months then consider indefinite with periodic bleed-risk review
Cancer-associated VTE -> extended DOAC (edoxaban or apixaban) or LMWH while cancer active
Extended-phase apixaban dose is 2.5 mg twice daily; rivaroxaban 10 mg daily
explanation.pearls: For provoked distal (calf) DVT, 3 months of anticoagulation is often adequate but shorter courses (6 weeks) may suffice for isolated calf DVT with a clear provoking factor and reliable serial imaging follow-up.

stem: You are the emergency department registrar. A 71-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 260 micromol/L, eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m2) is brought in by paramedics for progressive weakness over 2 days. He takes perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K supplementation for prior hypokalaemia (last review 6 months ago). ECG on arrival shows peaked T waves in V2 to V5 and a prolonged PR interval of 240 ms. He is awake, chest is clear, no ischaemic chest pain, blood pressure and heart rate are stable. Point-of-care venous gas gives potassium 7.4 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 138/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) on VBG, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 340 micromol/L (60-110) vs baseline 260, glucose 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), pH 7.28 (7.35-7.45), ECG peaked T waves V2-V5 and PR 240 ms
data_table.History: CKD stage 4 baseline creatinine 260, medications perindopril, spironolactone, slow-K, no chest pain, no diabetes-related hypoglycaemia risk

lead_in: Which intervention should you perform FIRST?

options.text: Give intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 20 minutes as the initial hyperkalaemia therapy
options.rationale: Insulin-glucose shifts potassium intracellularly and is a subsequent step, but does not immediately stabilise the myocardium. In the presence of ECG changes, calcium is given first because cardiac stabilisation cannot wait for the 20-30 minute onset of insulin-driven shift. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes with continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring
options.rationale: With hyperkalaemia and ECG changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation), calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2 to 5 minutes is the first-line intervention to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Onset is within 2 to 3 minutes and duration is 30 to 60 minutes. Subsequent steps shift and remove potassium. Cease perindopril, spironolactone and slow-K; consider renal replacement early in dialysis-eligible CKD stage 4. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as the initial intracellular potassium-shift therapy
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly and can reduce serum potassium by 0.5 to 1 mmol/L, but the onset is 15 to 30 minutes and it does not stabilise the myocardium during that window. It is adjunctive after calcium and insulin-glucose. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Give oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g with sorbitol as the initial potassium-removal therapy
options.rationale: Cation-exchange resins remove potassium slowly over hours and do not address acute myocardial risk. Their efficacy and safety are also debated (colonic necrosis) and they are not the first step in acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: eTG Fluids and Electrolytes: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Call renal services for urgent haemodialysis today and defer any other therapy until dialysis can start
options.rationale: Dialysis is often the definitive treatment for CKD stage 4 with symptomatic hyperkalaemia unresponsive to medical management, but arranging dialysis takes time. Immediate myocardial stabilisation with calcium cannot be deferred. (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, calcium gluconate is given first to stabilise the cardiac membrane. Insulin-glucose (with or without salbutamol) then shifts potassium into cells. Definitive removal is achieved by cessation of contributing agents, potassium-binding resins or haemodialysis. In CKD stage 4 or 5 with severe or refractory hyperkalaemia, early nephrology involvement for haemodialysis is essential.
key_points: Any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes -> calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV first
Then insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL 50% glucose over 20 min (monitor BSL 1-2 hourly for 6 h)
Adjunct salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised for additional potassium shift
Definitive removal: cease offending drugs, potassium binders, haemodialysis if refractory or CKD
explanation.pearls: Insulin-glucose hypoglycaemia risk peaks 1-2 hours post-dose; monitor blood glucose for at least 6 hours after administration.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in an emergency department. A 14-year-old girl (weight 42 kg) presents 15 minutes after eating a peanut-contaminated dessert at a birthday party. She has known peanut allergy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy for which she takes atenolol 25 mg daily. Her mother administered her EpiPen 300 mcg intramuscularly 3 minutes ago on the way in. On arrival she has stridor, generalised urticaria and is agitated. Blood pressure is 78/44, pulse 96 with poor volume, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on room air, wheeze and mild subcostal recession, and hoarse voice. She is not yet cyanotic and remains alert. A second IM adrenaline dose has just been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, mild angioedema of lips, stridor with hoarse voice, wheeze with mild recession, cool peripheries, no cyanosis, alert and following commands
data_table.Medications: Atenolol 25 mg daily for HCM, EpiPen 300 mcg IM given by mother at scene, further 300 mcg IM given at arrival

lead_in: Despite two IM adrenaline doses she remains hypotensive and stridorous. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are adjunctive and do not treat immediate airway or circulatory compromise. Onset is delayed by hours and they have no role as second-line management of acute anaphylaxis with persistent hypotension. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer intravenous chlorphenamine 10 mg over 5 minutes as second-line therapy for refractory anaphylaxis
options.rationale: Antihistamines relieve urticaria and itch but have no effect on airway obstruction or hypotension. They are not first- or second-line in refractory anaphylaxis and should never delay adrenaline infusion or fluids. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Start intravenous adrenaline infusion plus a 20 mL/kg saline bolus, and prepare glucagon for beta-blocker refractoriness
options.rationale: In refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses, ASCIA guidance is to move to IV adrenaline infusion titrated to response (start 0.1 microgram/kg/min), give a 20 mL/kg saline bolus for hypotension, and specifically in patients on beta-blockade with refractory hypotension consider glucagon 1 to 5 mg IV (paediatric 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a maximum of 1 mg) followed by infusion because glucagon bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via cAMP. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg on high-flow oxygen and defer any further intramuscular adrenaline dosing
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol may help wheeze but does not address stridor, laryngeal oedema or hypotension. Adrenaline remains the definitive agent for anaphylactic airway and circulatory compromise. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

options.text: Perform emergency needle cricothyroidotomy given the stridor and hoarse voice suggesting laryngeal obstruction
options.rationale: Definitive airway is escalated when medical management fails to reverse laryngeal oedema and the airway is becoming unsustainable. Cricothyroidotomy is a last-resort rescue after failure of medical therapy and attempted intubation, not the immediate next step while pharmacological options remain available. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Refractory anaphylaxis after two doses of IM adrenaline requires escalation to IV adrenaline infusion and adjunctive volume resuscitation. Beta-blocker-treated patients may fail to respond to adrenaline, and glucagon (1 to 5 mg IV in adults; 20 to 30 microgram/kg to a max 1 mg in children) bypasses beta-adrenergic blockade via direct activation of cardiac cAMP. All patients require observation for at least 4 hours after resolution because of biphasic reaction risk.
key_points: IM adrenaline 10 mcg/kg (max 500 mcg) via ASCIA banded table is first-line; repeat every 5 min
Refractory shock or stridor: IV adrenaline infusion 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated to response
IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus for hypotension, repeat as needed
Beta-blocked refractory anaphylaxis: glucagon 20-30 mcg/kg IV (max 1 mg) then infusion 5-15 mcg/min in adults
explanation.pearls: ASCIA EpiPen banded table: 150 mcg for 10-20 kg (EpiPen Jr), 300 mcg for 20+ kg (EpiPen); never use 10 mcg/kg arithmetic in a real event.

stem: You are the paediatric consultant in a community adolescent mental health clinic. A 15-year-old girl has moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder confirmed on structured assessment. Symptoms have persisted 5 months. She has completed 12 sessions of CBT with a skilled psychologist without meaningful change in her PHQ-A score (still 17). She has anhedonia, hopelessness, weight loss, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan. She has no bipolar family history, no manic features, no psychotic symptoms, and no substance use. She has never taken psychotropic medication. Baseline ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms and normal FBC, UEC, TFTs. She and her mother are willing to consider medication with regular clinic review.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 68, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-A 17 (moderate-severe), TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count within normal limits, electrolytes within normal limits, ECG sinus rhythm QTc 410 ms
data_table.History: 12 sessions of CBT with psychologist without change, anhedonia, weight loss, passive suicidal ideation without plan, no bipolar history, no substances, no medication

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Citalopram 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Citalopram is not first-line for adolescent depression in Australia. RANZCP guidance and TGA-approved indications point to fluoxetine as the first-line SSRI with the strongest paediatric evidence base and TGA approval for use in this age group. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg once daily titrated to 50 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Sertraline is used as second-line in adolescents when fluoxetine has failed or is not tolerated. Fluoxetine is preferred first-line because of the strongest paediatric RCT evidence (TADS) and TGA registration. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Venlafaxine XR 37.5 mg once daily titrated to 75 mg once daily over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring
options.rationale: Venlafaxine is not first-line in adolescents because of higher rates of hypertension, discontinuation symptoms and increased signal for suicidal ideation in paediatric RCTs. It is reserved for treatment-resistant cases with specialist supervision. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Fluoxetine 10 mg once daily titrated to 20 mg once daily over 1 to 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent moderate-severe major depressive disorder after failure of an adequate psychological therapy trial. TADS demonstrated superiority of fluoxetine plus CBT over either alone and TGA registration supports use in this age group. Starting at 10 mg daily and titrating to 20 mg after 1 to 2 weeks reduces initial activation. Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation is required in the first 4 to 6 weeks per RANZCP guidance. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

options.text: Mirtazapine 15 mg nightly titrated to 30 mg nightly over 2 weeks with weekly monitoring for adverse effects
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has limited paediatric RCT data and is not endorsed as first-line in adolescents. Weight-gain and sedation side-effect profile also disfavours it in an adolescent with existing weight loss where activation is desired. (Source: RANZCP Depression in Youth)

explanation.summary: Fluoxetine is the first-line SSRI for adolescent major depressive disorder failing an adequate trial of evidence-based psychological therapy such as CBT or IPT-A. TADS demonstrated combination of fluoxetine plus CBT is more effective than either alone. Weekly monitoring for treatment-emergent suicidal ideation is mandated for at least 4 weeks after starting. Full antidepressant effect is assessed at 4 to 6 weeks.
key_points: Adolescent MDD first-line pharmacotherapy: fluoxetine 10 mg titrated to 20 mg
Combine with evidence-based CBT or IPT-A (superiority over either alone in TADS)
Weekly monitoring for suicidal ideation for first 4-6 weeks after starting SSRI
Sertraline is second-line adolescent SSRI; escitalopram third-line specialist choice
explanation.pearls: TADS trial: fluoxetine + CBT 71% response, fluoxetine alone 61%, CBT alone 43%, placebo 35% at 12 weeks. Combination is preferred whenever both are available.

stem: You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 5-month-old infant brought to the emergency department by his mother, who says he rolled off the bed 30 minutes ago. He is now crying but consolable. On examination there is bruising over the right cheek and behind the left ear, a small oval bruise on the anterior chest wall, and swelling of the right thigh with reluctance to bear weight on that leg. A brief screen shows he cannot yet roll from prone to supine or supine to prone. The mother appears anxious and the father sits quietly separated from the family. Radiograph of the right femur shows a mid-shaft spiral fracture. There is no prior child protection concern documented in the state health record.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bruises over right cheek, behind left ear, anterior chest oval bruise; right thigh swelling with reluctance to bear weight, moves other limbs symmetrically; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; developmentally cannot yet roll
data_table.Investigations: Right femur radiograph shows mid-shaft spiral fracture, full blood count within normal limits, coagulation profile within normal limits, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Reassure the family and apply a temporary femoral splint with orthopaedic fracture-clinic review at 24 hours
options.rationale: The pattern here (bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head sites, and a long-bone spiral fracture with a history discordant with the child's developmental stage) meets multiple red flags for inflicted injury. Discharging without paediatric admission, safeguarding involvement and full skeletal survey would fail the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Test for osteogenesis imperfecta and copper deficiency before considering any child protection notification
options.rationale: While metabolic and skeletal disorders (osteogenesis imperfecta, copper deficiency) are on the differential, they are investigated in parallel with, not before, mandatory child protection notification and admission. The child's protection cannot wait for a genetic workup. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Send the infant home with mother once the femoral splint is applied and give safety-net telephone advice only
options.rationale: Discharge home is unsafe when inflicted injury is suspected. The child requires medical admission for full evaluation, protective placement decisions and clarity around safe custody. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Ask the mother to leave the room and ask the father directly whether he shook or dropped the child in question
options.rationale: Confronting either parent alone in the emergency department without a structured multidisciplinary approach can compromise the child's safety, the investigation, and the parent's rights. Assessment is done in a structured setting through the child protection service. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

options.text: Admit for evaluation, notify state child protection today, and arrange skeletal survey plus CT head plus eye review
options.rationale: This infant has multiple red flags for inflicted injury: bruising in a pre-mobile infant, high-risk anatomical sites (torso, ears, head), a long-bone fracture at an age when the child cannot yet self-mobilise, and a history discordant with developmental stage. Australian and RCH guidance mandates admission, statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor as a mandatory reporter, and a full skeletal survey in infants under 2 years, with non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology examination to look for occult subdural haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhages. (Source: RCH CPG: Child Abuse)

explanation.summary: Bruising in a non-mobile infant, torso and head site bruising, and long-bone fracture with a history inconsistent with the child's developmental stage are strong indicators of inflicted injury. Immediate steps are admission for a safe environment, mandatory statutory notification to the state child protection service by any doctor, and a comprehensive investigation cascade (full skeletal survey, non-contrast CT head, dilated ophthalmology for retinal haemorrhage). Alternative explanations are investigated in parallel, not before, safeguarding.
key_points: TEN-4 FACESp bruising rule: bruises to torso, ear, neck under 4 years or any bruise in infant <4 months warrants NAI evaluation
Full skeletal survey mandatory in <2 years with suspected inflicted injury
Non-contrast CT head and dilated ophthalmology exam to detect occult subdural + retinal haemorrhages
Mandatory reporter notification is a legal duty; not dependent on caseworker approval
explanation.pearls: Fractures with high specificity for inflicted injury include metaphyseal corner (classic metaphyseal lesion), posterior rib, scapular, spinous process and sternal fractures.
